title: Antiepileptic Drugs in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A clinician‑oriented overview of how to choose, start and monitor antiepileptic therapy for children in low‑resource settings, focusing on common aetiologies, practical investigations and safe drug selection.

sections.p: Epilepsy is a disorder of recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal neuronal firing. Diagnosis requires ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one seizure with high recurrence risk (e.g., EEG epileptiform activity).
b: Seizure types: focal, generalized, unknown onset
In children, febrile seizures are excluded unless they become afebrile and recurrent

sections.p: Severity is gauged by seizure frequency, duration, and impact on development. The ILAE 2017 classification grades epilepsy as: (1) Controlled, (2) Drug‑resistant (≥2 appropriate AEDs failed), (3) Refractory with neuro‑cognitive decline.
b: Drug‑resistant if seizures persist after adequate trials of two tolerated AEDs
Refractory epilepsy often needs referral for surgery or ketogenic diet

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the leading aetiologies are structural (perinatal brain injury, neuro‑cysticercosis), infectious (malaria, cerebral malaria, HIV encephalopathy, tuberculous meningitis), metabolic (hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance) and genetic.
b: Perinatal hypoxic‑ischemic injury – common after home births
Neuro‑cysticercosis – focal seizures, often in rural areas
HIV‑related encephalopathy – consider in any child with HIV
Malaria – seizures during acute illness, may evolve to epilepsy

sections.p: Children may have staring spells, automatisms, tonic‑clonic jerks, or brief focal motor events. Look for post‑ictal confusion, injury, or regression in milestones.
b: Generalized tonic‑clonic: loss of consciousness, rhythmic jerking, post‑ictal sleepiness
Focal motor: asymmetric limb jerks, may evolve to secondary generalisation
Absence‑type: brief staring, no post‑ictal sleep

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues (e.g., fever for malaria, growth failure for HIV) and treat presumptively while arranging referral.

t.b: Does the child have epileptiform activity? → Confirms diagnosis, helps classify seizure type
Are reversible metabolic triggers present? → Treat underlying abnormality before chronic AEDs

t.a: Neuro‑imaging (CT scan preferred where MRI unavailable)
t.b: Is there a structural lesion? → Guides choice of AED (e.g., avoid carbamazepine in focal lesions with secondary generalisation)
Is infection a precipitant? → Treat infection, may reduce seizure burden

t.a: Serum drug levels (phenytoin, carbamazepine) if available
t.b: Is the drug within therapeutic range? → Adjust dose or switch if sub‑therapeutic or toxic

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent care or suggest a non‑epileptic cause.
b: Status epilepticus (>5 min continuous or recurrent seizures without recovery)
New focal neurological deficit
Severe head trauma or fever >38.5 °C with seizures
Progressive developmental regression

sections.p: First stabilise the child, then start an appropriate AED based on seizure type, comorbidities and drug availability.
b: Choose a first‑line oral AED: phenobarbital (broad‑spectrum, cheap, available) for most children; valproate for generalized seizures if liver function normal; carbamazepine for focal seizures without secondary generalisation
Avoid phenytoin in children with cardiac disease (arrhythmia risk) and avoid valproate in girls of child‑bearing potential without folic acid supplementation

sections.p: Regular review every 3–6 months to assess seizure control, growth, and drug side‑effects. Counsel families on adherence, fever management, and avoidance of missed doses.
b: Monitor for sedation, rash, hepatotoxicity (especially with valproate)
Screen for cognitive or behavioural changes
Vaccinate according to national schedule; avoid live vaccines if on high‑dose steroids for seizures

sections.p: Conditions that mimic seizures can lead to misdiagnosis.
b: Psychogenic non‑epileptic attacks – normal EEG, prolonged duration, no post‑ictal sleepiness
Syncope with myoclonic jerks – brief loss of consciousness, rapid recovery
Movement disorders (e.g., dystonia) – stereotyped posturing, no loss of awareness
Normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy if clinical picture is convincing
Serum drug levels may be falsely low if taken too early after dose
CT may miss small cortical malformations that MRI would detect

whenToSeekHelp: Severe head injury or fever with seizures

faq.q: Can I use phenobarbital in a child with asthma?
faq.a: Yes; phenobarbital does not worsen asthma, but monitor for respiratory depression if high doses are needed.
Valproate is teratogenic; it increases risk of neural‑tube defects, so high‑dose folic acid and alternative drugs are preferred.

faq.q: What is the first step if a child presents in status epilepticus?
faq.a: Give an IV benzodiazepine immediately, then secure airway and start a longer‑acting AED.

exam: What immediate drug would you give to a child in status epilepticus and why? — IV benzodiazepine; rapid GABA‑mediated inhibition stops seizure activity.

A 4‑year‑old with focal seizures from a neuro‑cysticercosis lesion is not responding to phenobarbital. Which AED is preferred and why? — Carbamazepine; effective for focal seizures and inexpensive, but avoid if lesion causes secondary generalisation.

Explain how you would differentiate a psychogenic non‑epileptic attack from an epileptic seizure in a low‑resource ward. — Look for prolonged duration, lack of post‑ictal sleepiness, normal EEG during event, and stress triggers.
A child on valproate develops mild transaminase elevation. What is your next step? — Continue if <3× ULN and asymptomatic, repeat labs; if >3× ULN or symptoms, switch to alternative AED.

Why is folic acid supplementation essential for children on chronic antiepileptic therapy? — Antiepileptics can impair folate metabolism, increasing risk of anemia and, in females, neural‑tube defects in future pregnancies.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a child presents with a first generalized tonic‑clonic seizure and fever. How do you manage? — Treat malaria promptly, give a single dose of IV benzodiazepine for seizure control, then start a short course of phenobarbital if seizures recur.
List three red‑flag features that would prompt urgent referral to a tertiary centre. — Status epilepticus, new focal neurological deficit, rapid developmental regression.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of phenobarbital as a first‑line AED in low‑resource settings? — Advantages: cheap, broad‑spectrum, long half‑life; Disadvantages: sedation, behavioural effects, potential respiratory depression.
